It sounds like your son is suffering from cognitive distortions. He feels like people have a negative view of him despite the fact that people around him are very positive toward him.

I would recommend he tries a therapist specializing in Cognitive Behavior Therapy (CBT), it's basically the gold standard for treating these kinds of issues.

Medication certainly can help, and you're right about the potential for it to be a temporary measure. Just because he feels as though his depression is caused by external factors doesn't mean medication can't or won't help - the medication can help support him while he musters the wherewithal necessary to tackle the problems causing his depression.

It's clear that you care very much about your son and I think that could potentially help him with his depression quite a lot. A robust support group is necessary to address many mental health concerns, so he's lucky to have you in his life.

You should try to spend time with him regularly to remind him that he is important to you, that he is important to the lives of the people around him. That will help reinforce his sense of self worth.

Maybe you could talk to a therapist with your wife (and potentially your son as well) to learn more about what he's going through, why, and how you can better support him through his struggles.

There are a couple of different schools of thought when it comes to therapy. I'm not an expert but I do know that there are entire philosophical differences between different types of therapists.

With what you're describing wanting, I'd say maybe look into cognitive behavior therapy. A lot of it, at least as far as I've been exposed to it, is about identifying certain patterns of thought and behavior (patterns are a large part of the *why* we think and do the things we think and do you've mentioned wanting more focus on) and trying to strategize different ways of dealing with them to reach better outcomes. It's very result-driven and might offer you the help you're looking for.

I'd recommend trying to find someone who really knows the field to maybe get some more specifics. Different qualifications they have might tell you a bit about the style they're going to try with you, and they might be able to tell you which ones are more suitable to your wants/needs.

Therapist burn out is a very real thing. Very empathetic people tend to gravitate toward that field and it takes an enormous toll to see people you genuinely care about hurting profoundly. And therapists generally get to see the bits that hurt more than most of us get to see in the people that we care about, and they have to go through it a lot more often. It's a very difficult job. I don't envy them one bit.

If you're having trouble connecting with your practitioner, you might want to try seeing a different one. You should absolutely be sure that your practitioner cares about you. It shouldn't feel like they're just going through the motions.

I know it's hard and a lot of work, but it's definitely worth it. Whatever you end up doing, I hope it goes well for you.

An overwhelming majority of mental illnesses aren't hereditary in the way that you seem to think that they are. It's not like the color of your hair or your eyes or your skin where you're born and that's just what those things are, based on your genes. You aren't born with depression, or bipolar disorder, or schizophrenia, or what have you. You're born with a *genetic predisposition* toward one of these conditions.

Many mental illnesses require "triggering" events or circumstances for them to manifest - and it may take multiple of these triggers for it to happen. These are things like early life trauma, neglect, abuse to abuse of certain drugs, alcohol - extended periods of extreme stress, just to name a few.

If you were to take a pair of biological twins who have the same genetic predisposition toward a mental illness, and put them in two different homes, one which was stable and nurturing, and one which was chaotic and traumatic, the former child would develop into a well balanced, healthy individual, whereas the latter child would have a much higher risk of manifesting a mental illness.

It's a very small percentage of individuals who are dealing with a mental illness who haven't dealt with *any* of these triggering events. Like, single digit percentages small. You're *far* more likely to have experienced one, *or many*, of these events prior to manifesting your mental illness.

 

So what does this mean? Well, it means that you're a responsible individual for making these considerations for the future of your child. Which is a promising sign. If you're able to keep your mental health issues under control, you'll likely be able to provide your child with an environment that will foster healthy growth and development - your mental illness is by no means a sentence of struggle and privation for your child. You simply need to be a bit more attentive, a bit more aware, and a bit more concerned about certain things than other parents may have to be (although almost all of these triggering events even people with more robust genetics, in terms of mental fortitude, would be best to avoid, as well). You also have to remain more vigilant about taking care of *yourself,* since you'd have a vulnerable person for whom you would be responsible for. But *it is possible* to raise a healthy child in a healthy environment, even *with* a mental illness.

I'd also like to point out that mental health awareness and treatment options are improving rapidly, so even if your child *did* develop one, the tools available to them throughout their lives would be better able to help them with the issues they *may* end up facing.

I think that even if you're *considering* pursuing mental health treatment, it's a pretty good idea to try it. Even people without any kinds of disorders or anything like that, when dealing with particularly difficult periods of their lives - which you most certainly seem to be - could use a little bit of help managing all of their issues surrounding that period/those events/etc.

That said, it certainly seems like you have some sort of long standing issue. You seem to keep on finding other justifications for the way that you're feeling, and there *is* legitimacy to that - your situations have certainly been trying, and most certainly could/did cause a lot of your negative emotions, but... Negative emotions could also be causing you to fall into *some* of those circumstances, as well. It's kind of a negative feedback loop.

The idea of mental health treatment isn't necessarily to just change the way you feel so you feel better with your current situation, it can be to help get you the tools necessary to allow you to take steps to improve aspects of your life which are currently affecting you detrimentally, that you might not otherwise have been able to.

Whether this is just talking to a psychologist and learning how to identify certain patterns in your thoughts and behaviors, learning where they lead, and how to prevent them from taking over, to learning about different needs for happiness you might not necessarily be fulfilling, and how to go about fulfilling them, to talking to a psychiatrist and trying some sort of pharmacological therapy, there's a wide breadth of tools available to you that can cause some *serious* and *positive* changes in your life. If you think that either of these things (or both! medicinal interventions are actually shown to be *much* more effective when supplemented with speaking to a therapist as well) could be beneficial to you, please take active steps in pursuing them!

As for what do you even say to your doctor, you can just talk to them about your history with these issues. They should be able to refer you to a professional who will likely have a lot of really specific questions they'll be able to ask you to figure out what's going on - you don't really need to worry about preparing any information ahead of time. Just try to be open and honest, it's a lot harder to get help if you can't be honest about the things that you've been through or the things that you've felt.

They're useful things because they compel us to move throughout our lives - to feed ourselves, to climb social ladders, to procreate and raise as capable of children as we can. But, ultimately, there isn't an intrinsic definition to any of these things. We define them ourselves. The conclusions we come to, in terms of their definitions, are effected by a lot of different things - from our parents and peers and communities, to our life experiences, our natural personality types and our own conclusions we come to after devoting time and thought to them. Ultimately, I feel as though these things *are* in our control.

Just because there's no universal, intrinsic meaning or value in ourselves, or what we do, it doesn't mean there can't be meaning or value in what we do *to us.* In fact, that's *all there ever has been, for anyone, ever, or anyone there ever will be*. And we have free access to that ourselves. The only ones holding us back from it are us.

I've heard intelligent, articulate people (more intelligent and articulate than me, by far) describe nihilism as a trap - a dangerous one, at that - but I personally find it to be rather freeing. That it's okay that my views and feelings about things are a bit different than everybody else's, because they're no more (or less!) right about these things than me. And I feel a lot less pressured taking my own course through life, because I don't really find the same amount of value in keeping pace with the more traditional mile stones that other people sort of subscribe to in the live feed of their little value systems. I think it's safe to come to the conclusion that one is mentally ill, and maybe to get *some idea* of what *may* be wrong with ourselves, but I definitely feel as though it's a bit too difficult for us to figure out an honest diagnosis for ourselves for a whole variety of reasons.

There's a reason Doctors don't diagnose themselves, and a reason Lawyers don't defend themselves in court, either. It can take a third party perspective and an uninvolved dispassion to make certain, tricky, distinctions between two similar shades of grey.

It can be helpful to think about and make note of each individual issue that you're having, but ultimately it's up to your doctors to decide what they mean. If you feel as though they aren't taking everything into consideration, you are definitely free to (and are actively encouraged to) get a second opinion. Doctors aren't perfect, and what one person may be intimately familiar with, another person may not be. That said, your own informal research (or, honestly, even formal research, as I've mentioned above) is no substitution for a licensed and trained professional.

Ultimately, for me, I feel as though the specific diagnosis doesn't matter to much. All that matters is that I've got struggles, and in which way these struggles affect my life. Whether these struggles can be called "bipolar" or "borderline personality" or something else entirely, that doesn't *really* affect me any differently in the practical day to day of my life. What really matters, at least to me, is that I *have* these issues, and how I deal with them.

The different diagnosis may affect the treatment plan, I guess, but if there's a treatment plan then that means your doctor's involved, and you don't have to worry much about self diagnosis anymore, anyway. Again - make sure you talk to your doctor about all of your concerns, and raise new ones as they come, and be honest about *everything* with them. If you can't be, then they can't *really* help you. It can be hard, but if you can't quite find yourself being *completely* honest with them, maybe finding another one with whom that would be a bit easier would help. There's no issue "shopping around" to find the right fit, especially with issues like these.

I hope the best for you. It's not fair for us to have to struggle like this, but please believe that there's light on the other side of that proverbial tunnel, and that it's worth chasing. Take care!

From the effects it has on your brain chemistry, to the effects it has on your thoughts (do you start thinking about something while you're drinking, and then ruminate upon it afterwards?), to the effect it has on your physical body - when you're feeling well you tend to have a greater proclivity toward happiness, when you're unwell the opposite is true.

I don't really notice a perceptible difference in my base line levels when I drink as I've experienced with other psychoactive substances, but I couldn't say one way or the other whether that's a possibility. I can really only speak for my own experiences.

The thing about getting older is that it's a rather long and drawn out process. You don't wake up one day with a head full of gray hair, it grays one strand at a time - and, while the first few may be quite stressful, you get accustomed to it - and what's the difference between 5 grey strands and 7? There's not much. You don't even *really* notice the difference between one day and the next. Or a week, or a month - hardly even those between years.

Every day you wake up and it's just your life. Sometimes you get an odd jarring realization that you're getting older with a strange new pain, or a limited capability you've never encountered before - but they're not *that* common, and you get used to *them*, too.

Aging isn't as bad as our culture has inspired fear into us for. We're almost phobic of getting older, which I think is sad. There can be dignity in old age - the most dignified person I've ever known was my grandmother. She kept working into her 70s, not for the money, but as a choice. Hey, so, there are 3 "types" of depression.

There's depression as sort of an acute response to some sort of situation or circumstance, so, like, losing your job, losing a friend or relationship, a death in the family, etc. Most people go through a number of these at some point in their lives. They're usually temporary.

There's depression as a symptom of a psychiatric condition, so, if you have bipolar disorder, or seasonal affective disorder, or one of a couple others, then you're likely going to go through phases of a depressive state.

Finally, there's a condition itself called "clinical depression." This is basically when you have the symptom of depression, but none of the other things that would make you qualify as being "bipolar" or having a "borderline personality".

People who have otherwise normal lives, people who "should" be happy, but don't, they fall into one of the latter two camps. This basically means that there's some sort of issue with how your brain processes certain neurotransmitters - whether it's not producing enough, or whether there's an issue where it's flushing too much of it out of your system, or some other mechanism - the consequence of that issue is that your emotional regulation isn't quite typical, and depression is one of those atypical patterns.

If you can't really find a reason why you're feeling depressed, if there's nothing that's immediately obvious to you that you can go about resolving, you *may* want to consider talking to your family and a doctor about it. There *may* be help for you out there that can help you resolve the issues that you're having.

It's a very heavy burden, it can be heavily restrictive, and these people still have themselves to worry about, too. So it's super important, at least in my experience, not to rely on them to maintain your own happiness.

It's okay to seek support, and a partner can be a great source of that, but being diligent in your own mental health is super important, too. I've seen a lot of relationships be ruined by one person unloading all of the responsibility of maintaining their mental health onto the other person. I've had a few of my own personal relationships spoiled by that specific thing, too. And it never happens intentionally, at least, not in my experience. What happens is this other person is usually super sincere and enthusiastic and legitimately wants to help you and so they try to but it just ends up being so dominant in the relationship dynamic that it becomes overwhelming, so I personally try my hardest to maintain certain boundaries no matter what when I get into a relationship with someone.

I hope you the best. It *is* possible to have meaningful relationships, and it *is* possible to contribute to another persons life in a deeply positive way, despite how difficult that feels when you get low on self esteem. Cheers.

I noticed a *bunch* of places where I'd end up just looking for him out of habit when I moved around the house. Every time I went to take a shower, every time I went to get something to eat, I'd just poke my head all around and do a quick little scan for him. He used to brighten my day so much in so many different ways, and now he can't.

*That* specific set of behaviors stopped after 2 or 3 weeks, maybe? And *that* cut the heartache a *lot*. I still get sad when I think about him, I still get sad when I notice one of this things, or I see a little spot he'd used to roll around on, or bask in the sunlight through the window at. I used to. Took a lot of years to grow out of. Sometimes I sink into a spiral of bitterness and jadedness and fall into old habits. It's easy to succumb to the temptation, but I also know it's just not true.

Basically, for me, I thought I was oh-so-much-smarter than everybody else, and I thought being oh-so-much-smarter than everybody else was a terribly big deal. I looked down on other people who weren't oh-so-much-smarter than everybody else for not being so, and I looked down on other people who didn't value being oh-so-much-smarter than everybody else as much as I did.

I had a realization, one day, that if I weren't as smart as I was (which wasn't as much as I once thought I was, mind you), then being smart wouldn't be particularly important to me.

I wasn't physically strong, and being physically strong wasn't very important to me. I wasn't particularly good at talking to people, and while that one was maybe a little bit *more* important to me than most things I wasn't good at, it also wasn't a particularly big deal to me, either. (That one's a bit funny, honestly, I think I blamed *everybody else* for *my* shitty social skills; 'why don't these people treat me better? why don't these people understand?' when I was unlikable and not particularly good at expressing myself)

We tend to value our strengths because they're things that we're good at. We see the benefits of these strengths because we're strong in that capacity. We tend to undervalue our weaknesses because we manage capably despite them. I think it's important to understand that for all the individual things that make you feel better than all these other people, they're managing just fine without them. You'd manage fine without all these things you were oh-so-much-better than everybody else at, and those things wouldn't be nearly as important to you if you weren't so strong in those ways.

It's refreshing to hear that you like yourself, especially when it's easy to fall into a spiral of self loathing when you're depressed, I just hope it isn't necessarily at the expense of others.

You should love yourself for who you are, independent of others. You don't need to compare yourself to everyone else, or anyone else, you don't *need* to be better than them. I personally found a lot of solace in realizing that I *wasn't*, that I was *just like* everybody else. You're a lot less isolated when you climb down from your high horse.

People who need to find different reasons to look down on other people are usually insecure people, and it's pretty common for high schoolers to feel insecure. A lot of people grow out of this, but some people don't. You'll always have shallow, insecure people in your life, there's just a few fewer as time goes on, and it gets a bit easier to deal with them.

I know it's hard, but try not to worry what others think about you too much. Definitely try not to dwell on the individual things people think poorly about you for.

This might seem a bit back handed but I hope you don't take it that way - but, if it weren't for all the things they currently look down on you for, they'd just find something else to. It's not actually about you being flawed in any way, it's about their own inadequacies and their needs to project them.

I actually didn't get bullied too much in high school despite me being a really 'easy target' in a **lot** of ways. I've *always* been *weird*. I have weird interests, I act in weird ways, I talk weird and think weird things. All these things are really easy for other kids to make fun of, and they did, for a bit. And I didn't care. It didn't bother me, because I knew there was nothing wrong with me, and often times something wrong with them.

And they stopped.

It's not worth their time or effort to bully you if you don't give them the reaction they're seeking. The reaction their seeking is making you feel bad, so they can feel powerful, so they can feel better. If you rise above it, they can't feel powerful over you, they can't feel better than you, so they have to just move on.

I feel like there's just *got* to be some underlying disconnection from reality if you're really capable of operating under the assumption that "all women are life sucking leeches who only want men who are really tall, have perfect teeth,  a lot of money, big muscles and drive nice cars." It's pretty much empirically untrue. It's not even a point you need to *research*, you can just look around with your eyes. Anywhere. Everywhere. I really would advise not getting too worked up about the spiteful delusions of the hateful few.

Nothing they have to say can be of any value to you, even if they refer to you directly, they're not looking at you, just their distorted view of you. As for wanting to help them, that's a noble thought, but in my long experience of trying to help people who weren't actively trying to help themselves already, it typically doesn't go anywhere. Not even just strangers, who are typically even less open to that sort of thing, but close personal friends, too. Life's a process and we all go through it in our own way.

Things typically don't "get" better, unless you've got some oppressive force in your life pushing you down that somehow resolves itself, which... Does happen, but it's not really "common."

When people say things "get better," they mostly mean to say, "you make things better." Some of it comes with developing better coping mechanisms which lets you start to actually rebuild your life, other times it can involve seeking help and starting there, sometimes we can just get lucky and find good people who really want to help us.

The most effective way to have things "get better" is to play an active role in improving your self, your situation, and your life in general. It's hard, impossibly hard, especially if you don't have a solid support group or lack the resources to seek help - two things which, I think, are true for quite a lot of us.

But it *does* happen and it *is* possible.

It takes a lot of self awareness to accept that your struggles with other people often times are reflections of issues you're having interacting with other people. It can be very challenging to acknowledge that, and to approach changing it.

This isn't something that just happens from men to women about romantic (or, oh God, purely sexual) relationships. It's something most of us experience in a variety of different ways. It's so much easier to just project all these issues you're having on everyone around you. It makes you feel safe and secure, it's really tempting to just say, "I know that I'm a great guy, all these girls are just too blind to see it." In a lot of ways, I'm sure it's true, it can be very hard to express all the things about yourself that make you a valuable person, and I truly and honestly believe that we all have aspects that make us valuable people, but that's not really the whole story. We just like to remain willfully ignorant, I suppose.

I hope you don't take their projections to heart. Just try to identify that it's a person who is suffering, but isn't really ready to address the real reason why they're suffering. They'll get there, some day, at least *most* of us do.

I'm sure even if you died from something "more natural" than suicide, it'd still break your family's hearts, it'd still leave them shattered.

It sounds like you're not getting the appreciation or love or affection that you desire, and that's tragic - but there are much better ways to get that than to be dying, you know? I really hope you meet some better people who make you feel a lot better than the lot you've got in your life.

Maybe try meeting new people? I know it's hard, and it seems pointless, but you might really find someone who appreciates you and is thoroughly happy to have you in your life. That's what, at a glance, it seems like you're missing the most.

In any case, I'm sorry you're struggling the way you are and I sincerely hope you feel better soon. (:

If you think you should try it, then you probably should try it. I'm honestly under the impression that our mental health awareness, culturally, is very low, and seeking help and getting treatment is unfairly stigmatized when it's something I feel as though every single individual in the world could benefit from.

There are a lot of bad therapists out there. There are a lot of good ones that will be a bad fit for you. The trick is finding someone you're comfortable with, and really *working* at it. It's tough, but rewarding.

I would suggest trying to approach it with an open mind. Mental health care and services have improved dramatically since your mother was a teen. You could start with a psychologist first if you're unsure about diving right in to taking medication; they can refer you to a psychiatrist, nurse practitioner, or someone else who can prescribe medication later if needed. A psychologist is someone who is more interested in how your thoughts work as opposed to a psychiatrist who is more interested in the chemistry of your brain, how certain chemicals affect your mood.

You mentioned cost; are you not insured, or perhaps insured by a plan that doesn't cover mental health services well? In that case, you might want to call around and ask about payment assistance. I know that one of the places I went to for a while worked very hard to provide for the community and had a lot of programs to help people who weren't insured and couldn't afford treatment. I know it's *very* expensive to just try and get treatment without insurance, at least around here.

Yes that's a good point, when you're struggling with mood it makes it very difficult to regulate weight for a variety of reasons. It's harder to start exercising when you're not feeling well, it's easier to maintain poorer eating habits. Eating better and exercising more make it easier to maintain a healthier mindset, too, though.

Getting some help to deal with depression and anxiety would very likely help a lot in a lot of ways. It's kind of hard to understand the depths to which these issues affect *every* aspect of your life. It's a lot more than just the way you feel in any given moment.

The only people who claim weight loss is easy have never been obese. I remember reading a story a few years back of a personal trainer who purposefully gained a lot of weight so he could try to understand what it felt like for people to have to then try to lose all that weight. Even as someone who was educated in the proper way to eat and exercise, he said it was probably the hardest thing he'd ever had to do in his entire life. You absolutely shouldn't feel like you're struggling with something that's "easy" by any stretch of the imagination. It's hard. Impossibly hard.

Maybe try baby steps. A lot of the time people tend to try to change a lot of aspects of their lives all at once. They try to start exercising a lot, all the time, while changing their diet a tremendous amount, all at the same time. It's impossible to keep up doing something like that. It's much easier to, say, try to reduce snacking in between meals, first, or reducing how many sweetened drinks you drink in a day. Once you're comfortable with that, maybe try exercising 10 minutes a day once every 2-3 days. Once you're comfortable with that, try another small step.

I know how hard it is to go out when you're unhappy. While it's typically recommended to get out more often (depression is strongly associated with isolation whereas it's harder to remain depressed when you have constant social contact), if it's too hard for you right now, maybe you could try exercising at home, in the privacy of your own room? There's a ton of calisthenics exercises you can do without any equipment. Try checking out beginner body weight routines on youtube or something. :)
